deep_why: This audit measures political content exposure and recommendation diversity by comparing algorithm outcomes on paired short and long videos from the same source. The core insight is that a matched comparison isolates algorithm behavior: when identical source content flows through two systems and produces different recommendations, the differences reveal each algorithm's actual filtering and ranking choices. This works because the paired design controls for content properties, making differences attributable to algorithmic logic rather than inherent video characteristics. By systematically comparing recommendations across many pairs, the audit surfaces how platform design shapes political information reach and echo chambers—the real-world consequence of recommendation choices at scale.

Knowledge-graph retrieval coupled with explicit timestamps solves temporal reasoning by breaking down time-dependent questions into a series of constraint-checking steps. The core computation is verifying whether facts align with validity periods and whether event sequences satisfy logical order. This works because time imposes a total ordering—events have definite before-and-after relationships, and this strict structure eliminates ambiguity that reasoning without time would face. By propagating temporal constraints through iterative retrieval, the system ensures each retrieved fact fits the temporal position where it's needed, accumulating evidence that respects causality and duration. This transforms fuzzy temporal understanding into precise deduction, enabling systems to plan actions and infer outcomes in scenarios where timing critically determines correctness.

Customer Lifetime Value prediction involves two distinct estimation problems: ranking users into tiers and refining predictions within each tier. The framework decomposes the task architecturally—separating a ranking module that sorts users by value level from a regression module that estimates value within each level. This separation works because ranking and regression solve different problems with different optimal parameterizations. The ranking module identifies the coarse structure (which users are high-value), and regression refines fine-grained differences within that structure; combining them through architecture rather than loss functions ensures each component focuses on its intended goal without conflicting gradients. By giving special attention to high-value users through targeted augmentation, the system balances competing demands—overall accuracy on the majority and precision on the profitable minority—avoiding the typical pitfall where optimizing one metric destroys the other.

The paper identifies a feedback loop where AI-generated content contaminates search results, which then feeds training data for new AI systems, which produces worse content, which further contaminates the web. The core dynamic is that search ranking algorithms cannot distinguish between human-authored and AI-generated text based on content quality alone when both are plausible. As contamination rises, diversity in retrieved results drops—search results increasingly resemble each other because they derive from the same AI sources rather than independent human perspectives. This matters because information retrieval's power comes from integrating evidence from multiple viewpoints; when most retrieved sources stem from a single AI system's output, that system's errors or biases corrupt all downstream reasoning. The analysis reveals that even when answer accuracy appears stable, the underlying evidence base has shifted toward synthetic sources, creating fragility invisible to traditional metrics.

Multi-armed bandit algorithms solve the core problem of choosing actions under uncertainty by balancing exploring new options against exploiting known good ones. The mathematical guarantee is that these algorithms achieve sub-linear regret—mistakes are bounded even without knowing payoffs in advance—because they track the performance of each option and gradually shift probability toward better-performing choices. This principle applies to agents making sequential decisions because each choice yields feedback (reward) that improves future estimates. When embedding bandits into language systems, text generation choices or content selections become arms, and user engagement or task success becomes reward. By treating agent decisions as a bandit problem, the system automatically learns which strategies work in its specific context while exploring enough to discover better approaches, enabling agents to adapt and improve without explicit reprogramming.

Advertising prediction models compute expected values that drive real business logic, so a single corrupted prediction can cause cascading harm in pricing and delivery. The system monitors whether current predictions match the statistical shape of healthy historical predictions—typically a log-normal distribution with a predictable tail. The core principle is that distribution shifts have detectable signatures: if corruption pushes predictions systematically higher or lower, or swells the tail, the aggregate distribution departs from the baseline. By comparing real-time distributions to historical ones using robust distance metrics, the system identifies when something has gone wrong without needing to pinpoint the exact failure. Once anomaly detection signals a problem, targeted mitigations (smoothing outliers, zeroing corrupted values) restore predictions to a healthy shape before they propagate into pricing and ranking decisions.

Toxic language detection fails on obfuscated variants because rule-based systems and static models cannot capture the full space of character substitutions and phonetic tricks. The framework represents toxic terms and their variants as a graph where nodes are expressions and edges encode relationships: visual similarity (similar characters), phonetic equivalence (pinyin substitutions), and contextual co-occurrence (words that appear together). This works because obfuscation preserves some invariant property—a visually similar character still resembles the original, a phonetic abbreviation still sounds the same—and these properties form detectable connections in the graph. By using language models to normalize input text and then querying the graph for connections, the system can recognize variants even when exact matches fail. When graph paths break (incomplete data), the system uses language models to reason through analogy, recovering likely forms and completing the picture.

Epidemic forecasting combines a mechanistic disease model (SEIR: susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered) with data-driven learning of spatial patterns. The core computation estimates flow rates—how fast disease spreads within and between regions. The SEIR model is sound because it describes disease dynamics as a flow system: susceptible people enter the exposed state at some rate proportional to contact, exposed become infected, and infected recover, with these rates determined by biological and behavioral factors. Learning these rates from data is feasible because spatial patterns encode information about local contact networks and transmission conditions. By integrating environmental, demographic, and entomological data into the graph neural network, the system learns how regional characteristics modify transmission rates, adapting the mechanistic model to local conditions rather than applying generic parameters. This marriage of mechanism and data learning lets forecasts adapt to emerging conditions while remaining grounded in disease biology.

Fashion attribute retrieval aims to find images where a specific style detail (sleeve shape, neckline, color) matches a query attribute. The challenge is that patches of fixed size often misalign with irregular regions—a collar might span across fixed patch boundaries, breaking attention mechanisms. Superpixels solve this by segmenting the image into irregular regions of uniform appearance, creating tokens that naturally align with semantic boundaries like collars or sleeve textures. The core principle is that superpixel regions respect edges in the image, so attributes (which are visual features) map cleanly onto superpixel tokens without requiring any learned alignment. An attribute-guided attention mechanism first identifies which regions are relevant to the query attribute, then extracts superpixel tokens from those regions, ensuring the transformer sees semantically coherent units. This eliminates background noise and focuses representation learning on regions that matter.

Crowdsourced labeling depends on worker quality, but existing incentive schemes either reward all contributions equally or ignore fraud. The framework computes each worker's contribution using signed Shapley values—a game-theoretic measure that assigns credit to players for their impact on outcomes. Unlike unsigned Shapley values, signed versions can assign negative credit when a player's data degrades model accuracy, capturing both helpful and harmful contributions. This works because Shapley values distribute credit or blame in a way that satisfies fairness axioms: a worker who consistently produces correct labels should earn more than one who produces errors, and this is reflected in their signed Shapley value. A stake pool mechanism then uses adaptive penalties and rewards tied to these values, creating incentives where honest workers gain and fraudulent workers lose money. By making incentives depend on actual outcome quality rather than just task completion, the system economically rewards good behavior and discourages bad behavior, improving labeling quality at scale.

Recommender systems suffer from data sparsity (most users rate few items) and class imbalance (popular items dominate, niche items are rare). The insight is to reformulate this as a node classification problem in a line graph—a graph where each node represents a user-item interaction (an edge in the original bipartite graph). Sparsity in the original graph becomes insufficient labeled nodes in the line graph, and imbalance becomes imbalanced label distribution in the line graph. This reformulation works because mature techniques for node classification and graph learning can now directly address these problems. By augmenting the line graph with synthetic nodes representing likely missing interactions and balancing the node classes, the system creates training data that covers sparse regions and underrepresented items without modifying the underlying recommendation model. This plug-and-play approach sidesteps the need to redesign the entire system.

This workshop entry is about curating critical review papers rather than novel methods. The value of review papers lies in distilling knowledge from multiple sources and perspectives into actionable insights, making research accessible to newcomers and practitioners. Reviews synthesize diverse findings to identify what works, why, and when, establishing foundations that guide future research. By creating a venue where such synthesis is evaluated and celebrated alongside novel contributions, the community elevates the meta-work of understanding—understanding how models fail, where datasets mislead, which approaches are reliable. This matters because premature deployment of poorly reviewed methods causes harm; rigorous critical analysis prevents this.

Industrial control systems have hard real-time constraints: sensor readings must complete within milliseconds, and delays can cause unsafe states. Blockchain consensus and homomorphic encryption introduce latencies of 51–440 milliseconds, violating safety margins by orders of magnitude. The paper's core insight is that security mechanisms must respect the system's timing boundary: if a safety-critical loop requires feedback within 10 milliseconds and a security operation takes 200 milliseconds, no amount of optimization can make the system safe because the loop will timeout before security completes. Lattice-based cryptography offers a lightweight alternative that computes authentication in microseconds, fast enough to fit within safety margins, while decoupling security layers—reserving heavy cryptography for non-real-time enterprise networks where latency is acceptable. This separation principle works because different parts of an industrial system have different timing requirements and threats, so security mechanisms should be tailored to each layer's constraints rather than forcing a uniform approach.

Search engines rank pages by matching query words and computing relevance; black-hat SEO exploits this by stuffing irrelevant pages with keywords to fool ranking. Language model-enhanced search engines add a filtering layer: they retrieve candidate pages, then synthesize summaries from the most relevant ones, filtering out low-relevance pages before synthesis. This filtering works because language models prefer information-rich sources—pages actually addressing the query—and marginalize keyword-stuffed noise that lacks coherent content. However, language model-enhanced search remains vulnerable to attacks that rewrite queries or segment malicious text to slip past filters. The paper evaluates this resilience systematically, showing that traditional SEO attacks largely fail (over 99% blocked) but rewritten-query attacks succeed at higher rates. This work reveals the threat surface of systems that combine retrieval and language understanding, enabling defenders to anticipate and patch failure modes.

Federated learning trains models on distributed devices without sending raw data to a server; edge-assisted systems introduce an intermediate aggregation layer. When client devices run different model architectures (heterogeneous models), standard averaging fails because incompatible architectures cannot be averaged. The framework deploys a fusion model on edge servers that learns to distill knowledge from heterogeneous client models into a unified representation. This works because knowledge distillation transfers what one model has learned into another model by matching output predictions rather than requiring identical architectures. A contrastive loss ensures the fusion model aligns with the global model, reducing the gap between edge-aggregated knowledge and cloud-aggregated knowledge. Block-based aggregation on the cloud then merges fusion models with different architectures by matching compatible component blocks. This hierarchical approach with intermediate representations lets the system accommodate device heterogeneity while maintaining global model coherence.
